George Berkeley

George Berkeley (1685–1753) radicalized empiricism into idealism: esse est percipi—to be is to be perceived 1. There is no “matter” behind our perceptions; the world just is the structure of experience. More concretely, his Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision 2 argued that visual depth is not directly given but inferred from cues such as ocular convergence, blur, and learned associations with touch—a constructive account of spatial perception that anticipates the cue-integration models of modern vision science.

David Hume

David Hume (1711–1776) pushed empiricism to its skeptical limits 3, 4. There is no substantial self, only a “bundle” of perceptions in constant flux. Causation is not observed in the world but projected onto it by the mind through custom or habit: having repeatedly experienced event AA followed by event BB, we come to expect BB upon seeing AA. This is, in modern terms, a description of learned predictive association—and Hume’s problem of induction (why should past regularities predict future ones?) remains the foundational challenge that Bayesian inference addresses but does not fully resolve.

La Mettrie

Julien Offray de La Mettrie (1709–1751) wrote what is arguably the most radical materialist text of the Enlightenment: L’Homme Machine 5. Humans differ from animals only in the complexity of their organization, not in kind. The soul is merely the brain in action; thought is a property of organized matter as surely as electricity is a property of certain materials. This thoroughgoing materialism—scandalous in its day—is the implicit metaphysics of modern neuroscience.

Condillac

Étienne Bonnot de Condillac (1714–1780) devised the celebrated statue thought experiment 6: imagine a marble statue endowed with a single sense, say smell. From this single channel, Condillac argued, the statue would gradually develop attention (by having one sensation more vivid than others), memory (by retaining faded sensations), comparison, judgment, desire, and eventually all the faculties of mind. This is a constructivist thought experiment in building a mind from sensory atoms—a philosophical precursor to the modern project of understanding how hierarchical world models are learned from raw sensory input.

Immanuel Kant

Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) produced the deepest philosophical foundation for the view of the brain as a world-modeler 7. Against the empiricists, Kant argued that the mind does not passively receive sensory impressions; it actively structures them through a priori forms of intuition (space and time) and categories of the understanding (causality, substance, unity, and others). Experience is always already a construction: what we perceive is not the world as it is in itself (Ding an sich) but the world as filtered through the mind’s own organizational principles (Erscheinung, appearance). The Kantian insight—that the mind brings structure to sensation rather than extracting it from a pre-given world—is arguably the single most important philosophical ancestor of predictive processing and the Bayesian brain.

Thomas Reid

Thomas Reid (1710–1796) mounted the most formidable 18th-century challenge to the “way of ideas” shared by Locke, Berkeley, and Hume 8, 9. Against the view that we perceive only our own mental representations, Reid argued that perception yields direct, non-inferential awareness of the external world. Sensation (a subjective feeling in the perceiver) and perception (a direct apprehension of an external object) are distinct acts that occur simultaneously but must not be conflated. For world-modeling theories, Reid articulates a perennial challenge: if perception is truly Bayesian inference over a generative model, why does it phenomenologically present itself as immediate, transparent contact with reality—rather than as the output of a laborious computation?

David Hartley

David Hartley (1705–1757) was the first philosopher to ground the laws of association in an explicit neural mechanism 10. Sensory stimuli produce vibrations in the nerves and brain substance; these vibrations leave behind diminished traces (vibratiuncles) that constitute ideas and memories. Ideas become associated when their corresponding vibrations co-occur, producing compound vibrations of increasing complexity from which all higher cognition is constructed. Hartley’s system—sensation as neural oscillation, memory as attenuated reactivation, and learning as temporal co-occurrence of neural events—is a recognizable ancestor of Hebbian synaptic plasticity and oscillatory neural coding, articulated more than a century before either.
